utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could hand you from yesterday afternoon Exhibit 926, which is, we hope, a complete copy of your report. Can you confirm for us -- my apologies for the problem yesterday afternoon. Can you not confirm for us that that is a complete copy of your report that you prepared as a result of your mission to the Vitez area of Bosnia and Herzegovina between approximately the 4th of May and the 11th or 12th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The report is, is it correct to say, several pages of observations and conclusions, if you will, followed by a series of appendices including the interview notes with various persons you spoke to as you described yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the Court's direction to move this along as quickly as possible, I have attempted once again to use a vehicle that hopefully will allow us to do that. I would ask for the usher to please distribute now what's been marked as Z858.2, and to the witness as well, please. Mr. President, if you will allow for the record, this basically outlines the principle points in an abbreviated direct or examination-in-chief that we want to put in front of Mr. McLeod, some of which largely speak for themselves, some of which we will ask to provide some further explanation or insight into. I will tell the Court that it either comes from his report itself, that is, the document which is Exhibit 926, or what we viewed as the most relevant excerpts from his testimony in the Blaskic case, simply again as a vehicle to move us along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where there is a reference to a report, there is no need to read it out again because we will have read it in the report. We can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand that. Obviously by way of presentation and emphasis from the Prosecution's case, this is an outline of the major points we would make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, do you have the outline Z858.2 in front you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mindful of the Court's admonitions, if you would look, please, at paragraphs 1 and 2? Can you please summarise briefly to the Court the more important parts of the basis for your reaching these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. These were the conclusions that I reached having been in the Vitez area, carried out all of my interviews, typed them up, thought about it, discussed my tentative conclusions with senior members of the ECMM headquarters back in Zagreb, and then pulled the whole thing together basically into one page which is at the front of my report, and so the conclusions that I reached, which you can see here, were the final thoughts that I had having seen everything, and having talked to everybody, and weighed up what I could see. I think it's fairly self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I may have omitted, and it's probably clear from the documents, but you were accompanied on this mission, among others, by another ECMM member, Mr. Friis-Pedersen, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Friis-Pedersen was a Danish monitor working in the Zenica regional centre, and I was accompanied by him or by Mr. Jean-Pierre Thebault, who was the head of that regional.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to points 1 and 2, can you tell us -- can you highlight for us some of the things that you either physically saw and observed while in the Vitez area or based on your interviews some of the points that led you to reach the conclusions stated in 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The events of the middle of April leading to up the 16th and after the 16th of April, '93, suggested there had been a long period of tension between the two ethnic groups in Central Bosnia. This appeared to have exploded on the morning of the 16th, and there were two versions of events which suggested that either one or the other party had been the instigators of the events. Eventually looking at everything and weighing it up, it seemed to be quite clear to me that the Croats had a political objective to attempt to implement the Vance-Owen Plan as this then stood in Central Bosnia, and they seemed to feel that in order to do that -- and the implication of that would have been they would have been able to establish political and military structures based on the ethnic composition of the canton, or cantons, as they were called, cantons, the areas that they controlled which would reflect the ethnic make-up of the area, and they seemed to believe that as long as the ethnic make-up of the area was almost entirely Croat, then they would be able to implement the Vance-Owen Plan and end up with structures which reflected their own ethnic make-up. In order to ensure that the Vance-Owen Plan would reflect a fundamentally Croatian population, they seemed to believe that they ought to get rid of the Muslim population. One can debate back and forth exactly how they were trying to do that, but it seemed quite clear to me that they were using, for example, the razing of Ahmici as an attempt to physically remove or kill off the Muslim population to allow them to then achieve their political objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me stop you there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Scott, the witness is saying that, in fact, it's a way of applying the Vance-Owen Plan. Could he specify exactly what he understands by that? Does that mean that this area was going to go to the Croats, according to that plan? Could we have more particulars on that? Does the witness think that this was a way -- he said it was a way of applying the Vance-Owen Plan. Could he explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you explain, in response to Judge Bennouna's question --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- what the Vance-Owen -- what the status of the Vance-Owen Plan was at this particular point in time, and I'm sure the Court would like it to be done somewhat briefly, and how that fit into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: My understanding, and it is now some time since I last looked at the documents, but my understanding of the Vance-Owen Plan was that they were attempting to create, right across Bosnia, political and military structures which would reflect the ethnic make-up, my understanding, that had originally existed across the country, and the intention was to stabilise events and then, amongst other things, hold elections and so on, to elect political bodies, having to establish them, and also to establish military and police structures that would reflect either Serb-controlled, or Muslim-controlled, or Croat-controlled areas, and where there was a clearly mixed operation, then these structures would have a mixed membership. I think that what the Croats were attempting to do was to ensure that in the areas where they wanted to have control, that they would, in fact, have a majority population when any elections were taking place. So I think that my understanding, my view, was that they were taking the intended political outcome and trying to move the population around to ensure that when they did actually implement the plan, the population would reflect their objectives. I gained the impression that they were trying to move slightly faster in their areas than the rest of Bosnia could move by saying, "We now have an area which is controlled by ourselves and which we are the majority ethnic group, and we would like to implement the Vance-Owen Plan now," which would then provide -- my view was is that they were then trying to provide some international recognition and legitimacy for what they were doing. Clearly, there were other areas which were Serb-controlled, for example, where it was simply impossible to try and do this, and they seemed to be trying to steal a march on the political process that was otherwise taking place around them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Usher, could you put a copy of this on the ELMO for the gallery and anyone who might not have a hard copy in front of them? (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We were considering, Mr. Sayers, the status of the evidence, because clearly the witness is giving evidence about matters which we are going to have to determine ultimately. They are matters which are in issue. As to whether there was such a plan is very much in issue, as I understand it. Now, one knows the rules about opinion evidence. The tentative view that we have come to about it is this, that while this witness's expertise is essentially that of a soldier, he was on the ground at the time, he had some experience as a European Monitor, and, therefore, we're prepared to admit the evidence of his opinions but on the understanding, of course, that these are matters which we have to decide, and it is entirely a matter for us what weight, if any, with respect to the witness we give to his opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on this, Judge May. I think you've actually anticipated the point that I was going to make. I'd just like to make that point and a different point. This gentleman has not been identified as an expert witness, and I understood yesterday that he was going to be permitted to give opinions relating to whatever military expertise that he has, but apparently he comes in today with panoramic opinions on sociological, political, and essentially the issues and the main point that is at issue. He's really giving a new expert report beyond and above what he's already provided to the Court in his one-page conclusions and appendices. I didn't want to let this go without an objection from our perspective for two reasons: First, it's beyond any competence that he has, beyond the military competence certainly; secondly, we have not had this gentleman identified as an expert witness, and certainly the Prosecution has had to do that since they've identified Dr. Donia as an expert and provided his report and followed the requirements of Rule 94 bis. Those are the only points that I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that we've given the ruling before the objection. No matter, I think it's going to be very much a matter of weight. As I say, the witness was there at the time. We've said he's entitled to express a view, but, of course, it's all subject to what weight, if any, we decide to give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you hear the way we intend to approach this. Perhaps, in light of that, you could take the matter very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm attempting to, Your Honour. I need to respond very clearly, Your Honour, and very briefly to two points. One is that this report has been provided and known to all the Defence. It was passed out as part of the supporting materials months, if not years ago. It is nothing new. The conclusions are not a new report. The conclusions stated in paragraphs 1 and 2 are stated on page 1 of this report. I just want to make that clear. He is not stating anything that has not already been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, let's move on. Let's not spend time on the procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, what did you see, for instance, in the village of Ahmici when you visited it on May the 4th which led you to believe that, in that particular instance, it involved what's come to be known as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: As we saw yesterday in the video clip very briefly, in fact, the video showed only a small portion of what happened, in the village, a large number of the houses had been burnt. There were still some houses which appeared not to have been touched at all. I understood, as we were going through the village, that the houses that hadn't been touched were occupied by Croats and the houses that had been destroyed had been occupied by Muslims. Most of the houses that had been destroyed had had their roofs burnt, as you saw yesterday on the video. Quite a number of the houses had contained bodies that had been burnt that were either discovered on that day or had been discovered previously by Colonel Bob Stewart. The reason why one could conclude that this appeared to be ethnic cleansing was that in most of the villages where that sort of activity had taken place, it was characteristic that houses would be destroyed by burning them as opposed to being destroyed by violent shooting. Again, there were clearly examples of villages which one saw which had been fought over extensively, and there, one would see that walls were pockmarked by bullets and so on, and in Ahmici, that simply wasn't the case. It appeared that a bunch of people had gone through the village systematically from house to house either evicting people or killing them in the houses and then burning the houses. Given that the preponderance of houses that had been destroyed were Muslim as opposed to Croat ones, which appeared not to have been touched, it seemed quite clear that it was the Croats who had done the destroying rather than the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, two points. I'm sorry. Number 1, I don't know about anyone else, but could you please try to keep your voice up maybe a bit and also for the reporter speak a little more slowly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall what the condition of the mosque in Ahmici was at the time of your visit, if you can tell us that briefly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The mosque had been attacked in some way, and the minaret had been blown up, so it was lying across the top of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Moving on to paragraph 3, what was the basis for your conclusion or characterising the attack on the 16th of April as "coordinated"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was basically in light of the reporting and briefing which I received from both the ECMM and UNPROFOR, particularly UNPROFOR, who had troops out on the ground and heard what was going on. They advised me quite clearly that attacks had broken out in a number of places at the same time, and that suggested that there was some form of coordination about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We will move through some of the items which we will not come back to specifically but the subject matter will come back up, 4, 5, and 6, without further commentary at this time, unless the Court has questions. Moving to point number 7, and before we get into point number 7, you stated a few moments ago that when you arrived in the Vitez area, there were essentially, I'm not back in the transcript, but something to the effect, Mr. McLeod, of two stories or schools of thought on what had happened, if I can say it that way.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what those schools of thought were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed, there were perhaps three different schools of thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The two most obvious ones were, first of all, that the Muslims had launched an attack on Vitez attempting to cut Vitez off from Busovaca, and that in the course of that attack, they had destroyed Ahmici; the second was that Ahmici had been destroyed by Serb special forces or agent provocateur in an attempt to destabilise the relations between the Croats and the Muslims in that area; the third version was that the Croats had launched an attack on the Muslims in an attempt to do something to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In reference to paragraph 7, two of the people you interviewed, is it correct, were Ivan Santic, the mayor of Vitez, and Pero Skopljak, who was the police commander in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Their explanation or story to you was that "As a result of a Muslim attack on the 16th of April, there had been a chaotic defence of Vitez in which the Muslims were displaced from their villages around Vitez," and you characterised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's an objection, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interfere, Your Honour, but we're dealing with a summary of what the Court has already read, and the question is pretty leading, and I object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the most non-controversial matter, really, about whom the witness met. Can we get on with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you view that assessment and the three schools of thought that you've just mentioned to us as incredible?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very simply, it struck me, having talked to people on both sides and talked both to Mr. Santic and also then Colonel Blaskic, who gave me almost exactly the same story, as impossible that the Muslims had been attacking the Croats who had been, according to their story, caught completely by surprise and had mounted a defence, if at the same time in Vitez, the Croats had been arresting a number of prominent Muslims. Because it struck me that if there had been a surprise attack mounted against the Croats, then they would have been defending themselves rather than rounding up people who were evidently in their beds, and equally, if there had been a surprise attack by the Muslims, and those very gentlemen would probably not have been asleep in their beds but would have been expecting something to happen. The story just didn't hang together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry, I have missed and I want, for the purpose of my note, to have the three schools of thought. These were what people told you on the ground?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what you base that on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The first school of thought was that the Muslims had launched an attack on Vitez to cut it off from Busovaca, in the course of which Ahmici had been destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. So that was a school of thought that the Croats were expounding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The second was, I think you said, that Ahmici had been destroyed by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, some of the Croats were suggesting that this was being done by agent provocateur from outside to try and just cause trouble between the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the third?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That the Croats attacked Ahmici, and Stari Vitez, and various other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to come back to the some of the points we just made, in a moment, if I can. Before we move forward in an effort at speed, and skipping over paragraphs 4, 5, and 6, let me say just so the record is clear, if you can glance back at those for one minute, those are your conclusions, and if we were to do it in a more traditional way this morning, that would be your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your interview with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak, was there anything else about -- did you observe any other conduct or statements by Mr. Santic, in particular, or both of them, or either of them, which cast further light on their outlook or policy toward the Muslims in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Santic spoke at great length and the details are all in my report. He started off by adopting what seemed to be a fairly balanced view which then, over the course of an hour or so, became increasingly extreme to the point where he was explaining exactly what he thought about what one should do with the Muslim population. It was he who set out in very clear detail his views about what should happen with the Vance-Owen Plan and its implementation. Quite early on -- or right at the very beginning of the interview, he identified my interpreter, who was a Muslim, and he appeared to be taking some pleasure in some of the things he was saying just to wind her up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to point 8, and I'm just pausing, Your Honour, just to give everyone a chance to look at that without reading it myself. In reference to your interview with Mr. Blaskic, can you tell us the various points or amplify, as stated here, on why you thought his position was, again, untenable?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Then Colonel Blaskic gave me, again, a very clear explanation of what he thought had happened during that morning, saying that he had been working from his bed and there had been this fighting that broke out, and they had mounted a defence of Vitez and various other places. His description of what happened thereafter all seemed to tie in with exactly what the UNPROFOR briefing had suggested, but it was quite clear that these people -- these Muslims had been arrested in Vitez that morning, because I met some of them and talked to them either in prison or out of prison, and the Croats didn't try and hide the fact that these people had been arrested that morning. As I've already said, I simply can't imagine how, if you're being attacked, you can, at the same time you're trying to defend yourself, start rounding up key individuals and imprisoning. So the logic of what Blaskic was saying just didn't tie together with the events which patently had been taking place that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, and the Court's, to appendix A2 of your report, Exhibit 926. It is -- excuse me, Your Honour. A2-1, the last four digits would be 7628, I believe. I hope. There may be -- again, Your Honour, due to different copying, there might be different numbers, but it is appendix A2-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the top of the page is that a list of the 13, as described here, leading Muslims arrested in Vitez on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list that was given to me by the Muslims, but the list seemed to be consistent and nobody seemed to be disputing the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we look toward the bottom half of that page, are those the positions that those people held in the community at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. What you've got down at the bottom of the page is the English translation of the titles which are written next to each of the names at the top half of the page. So I understand that's what the people actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your ten years of military experience, can you explain to the Court, please, the significance, from a military planning, coordination, and execution point of view of arresting 13 people about the same time, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It strikes me that to pick up that number of people, and I have -- I nearly had experience of doing the same thing in West Belfast, having prepared for an operation to go and pick somebody out of a pub. I eventually didn't actually do it. When we were doing it, we had about a couple of platoons, so about 60 people to pick up one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This was one man in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: One man in Northern Ireland. Slightly different warfare but the same basic principles applying. I imagine -- I don't know, but I can imagine how they could have used easily five people to pick up each of these, ten people perhaps. So you're soaking up 60, 130 of the Croatian forces. Colonel Blaskic had said that he had about 350 regular troops. I don't know whether these people are being picked up by the army or by the police, perhaps, but you're taking -- even if it's five people to arrest each individual, 65 -- that's 20 per cent of his total force. They were all picked up more or less at the same time in the morning apparently. That's the story which seemed to come from them as I spoke to them in the prison, and from everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would that indicate to you a certain amount of advanced planning and coordination?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't imagine how particularly if the Croats were under a surprise attack by the Muslims they could have taken a significant portion of their force to then go off around a number of houses and then arrest people, and to pick up 13 people, certainly had I been doing it, would have taken an awful lot of preplanning and preparation. It's not something that I think would have happened without anybody knowing about it. I simply can't imagine how that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Focusing your attention, please, on the last part of paragraph 8 where you say, "I find it extremely implausible," can you again, please, briefly amplify on that? What basis do you have for making that statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the suggestion was that Colonel Blaskic didn't know what was going on. Again, I can't imagine, given the position which I understand that he held, that an operation of this size could have been taking place without him being aware of it because, again, I don't know exactly how it was done but I can imagine that a significant portion of the troops available for the defence of Vitez, first thing in the morning, would have been deployed to go pick up people who appear to be very prominent members of the local population. If he was the boss, and he appeared to be the boss, then I can't imagine how it would have gone on without him being fully aware of what was going on and he probably having planned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Scott. I want to find out whether the persons who were picked up were confined to leading persons as you described them, on the basis of the information that you had. Were other persons picked up apart from leading personnel?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understand, and we could look at the note which I wrote at my meeting with the mayor of Vitez, that, in fact, a number of other people had also been detained or held in some way, because he made the point that, in fact, all of the other people had been released other than 13 who were being held. So I think, in fact, there were more than that but these were the key prominent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Robinson, would you like more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just very briefly looking back at paragraph number 4, of these 13, apparently two had been shot dead while being arrested, two by 11 May had been released, and the remaining, I guess it would be nine, were still in prison at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was my understanding of it. I certainly met one of the men who had been released, and I met a number of them in Kaonik Prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then go back to -- all right, moving forward then, paragraph 9 and 10 is your -- is an accurate statement of your position and you would so testify this morning?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've already made reference to other statements, explicit statements made by Mr. Santic earlier, and is it fair that the one cited in paragraph 10 would be one of those?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the sequence of your interviews, is it fair to say that you had spoke with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak immediately prior to speaking with Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to the observation made in point 11, would you draw any conclusion from Mr. Blaskic's statement at that time? I guess I'll say "Colonel Blaskic," given his rank at that time. Did you draw any conclusion from that statement made by Colonel Blaskic, based on your interview with him and with the other parts of your interviews and investigation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would have to be a fairly tentative conclusion but it struck me that he was a military man. We were having a conversation as an ex-soldier and a serving soldier. He didn't seem -- some of what he was saying suggested that he didn't seem totally comfortable with what was going on but he was clearly involved in doing it. There was such a marked difference between the view that he was putting across and the view that I just heard from the political -- Croatian political leadership in Vitez. Whereas normally I simply sat and listened to people and wrote down what they were saying, I actually challenged him and pointed out the fact that he was saying something which sound different. It may well have been that as a military man he was doing what he'd been told to do but some of what he was doing, presumably that would include things like Ahmici, he didn't feel terribly comfortable with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go on to point number 12. Is that an accurate statement? Is that your testimony this morning, to that effect?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I wrote in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By the way, can you tell the Court, did you have any understanding or come to know during your work in the Vitez area in May 1993, that you were being closely watched by the HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether there was a consistent programme to watch what was happening, but certainly when I stopped and talked to people on a couple of occasions and, again, it's noted in the report, at some point either the Croatian police turned up. In Busovaca, when I was talking to the imam, they actually came into his house and attempted to join in the conversation. Also in Vitez, when I went and talked to a gentleman, fairly rapidly somebody -- his neighbour came round just to find out exactly what was going on and the conversation stopped at both those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find that Mr. Sadibasic and his wife became very nervous when the neighbour appeared and the interview was terminated?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. They were extremely uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you identify who the HVO leader was who appeared at their house during the interview?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this stage I can't remember. We could check in the report to see whether I actually wrote down a name. He was identified as somebody who was a neighbour who was involved in the HVO, I think. He was certainly a Croat. He came round to find out what was going on. They became very uncomfortable, so we said, "Thanks very much," and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second incident that you mentioned, that would be found -- and for the Court's reference, I'm not suggesting you necessarily have to go there now, but this would be reflected in appendix P1 the interview of Mr. Sadibasic and, also, in appendix K1, which was the interview of the imam of Busovaca. Back on the second occasion, there were three HVO police officers who showed up while you were interviewing the imam?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that they were civilian police rather than HVO police but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. From the local Bosnian Croat government authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to paragraph 13. That is an accurate statement and would be your testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you just add to this in terms of what did you learn in terms of the authority or procedure, if you will, for members of the HVO to essentially, if I can use the term, check people out, to take people from Kaonik, prisoners, for the purposes of trench digging? What was the process for doing that, as you learned it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, there's a fairly lengthy conversation or interview we had with Mr. Aleksovski, who was running the prison. He made it quite clear that he was just doing his best as a professional gaoler, and that he was to a very large extent in the hands of the local HVO Brigade commanders, Busovaca and Vitez, and that they would either bring him people or from time to time they would take people away. He was quite -- he gave us an example of a release certificate being signed for somebody being taken away for a prisoner exchange, as far as I could see. I'm not entirely clear there was a routine for taking people out to dig trenches, although it was quite clear from what Aleksovski was saying that that was the case. From his description, I'm not quite clear whether actually it was the prison guards themselves who were taking people up on to the trenches. That's the impression that I was given, but certainly he was quite clear in some of his descriptions of what was happening, that they did take people up on to the front line and that occasionally -- he gave an example, there was fighting on the front line and they actually lost a couple of prisoners during fighting. It wasn't clear that they were either shot or they just ran away during the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether he described or did you come to know -- did the brigade commanders -- did someone at the brigade commander level have the ability to go to Kaonik and take prisoners or detainees out for various details?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not clear that at that stage that we were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on. Your full interview with Mr. Aleksovski is attached in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on to paragraph 14, the suggestion here -- there was a transfer -- some suggestion there was an attempt to move -- as you said earlier in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan. I apologise, Your Honour. I don't know how else to jump into this subject. Moving populations, various ethnic groups around to achieve the desired population make-up in a particular location, and that you talked about that earlier in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you find, during your work in May, 1993, that while there were apparently attempts to move Muslims out of areas, that it would appear there were also attempts to move some of the Croats from one area to another area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It was quite clear from both what I was told by the Muslim political leadership in Zenica and also by the reports from the ECMM, which are contained at the back of my report, that 2000 is the number that was being talked about. Croats had attempted to leave and then had left Zenica so the Muslim-controlled town to go back across the hill to Vitez and the suggestion was that they had been either advised, told, or had got the idea that it would be a good idea to move as a result of propaganda or information being disseminated by the Croats in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How would moving Croats out of a particular area be consistent with a plan, as you described it a few minutes ago, to implement the Vance-Owen Plan in a particular way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: It would have two effects. It would have the effect, on the one hand, of demonstrating that there were no Croats in the Muslim-controlled area. Therefore, that should remain a Muslim-controlled area. It would also have the effect, if you moved a significant number of Croats, additional Croats into what was otherwise, generally, a Croat dominated area that you would have even more Croats in that area which would make the ethnic mix even more clearly one-sided. If the idea was that you should prove that the ethnic mix in a particular area was predominantly Croat or Muslim, and then implement the plan so that you would have political and military structures dominated by that particular group, then that would fit exactly with what Mr. Santic, for example, was explaining to me is what they were trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you hear at the time or in your continuing work with Yugoslavia, as indicated in your background yesterday, did you ever hear the term of "self-cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't come across that as a term, but it's quite clear what I was describing could be termed as self-cleansing, where a particular population group is saying, "Well, for whatever reasons, we think we ought to move out of one area and into another area so that we can get the ethnic balance right".

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the latter part of paragraph 14, you make the statement or observation that many Croats did leave their houses as a result of propaganda they heard from Vitez. Is it correct that Vitez was a Bosnian Croat-controlled area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, that would be your testimony this morning, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's exactly what was in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What is the significance of or the conclusion you suggest by this observation, the fact that most of the Croat population had returned to their homes a short time later?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The clear impression which I was given, both by the Muslim political leadership and also by the ECMM working in the area and by the Catholic priests working with the Croatian population in the Zenica area, was that a number of things had happened which were clearly wrong in terms of people either being killed or moved out of their houses and their houses looted and so on, and that there's quite a lot of evidence that -- or the evidence that I was given is contained in the report, that people seemed to be attempting to stabilise the situation as best they could with the objective of having a multi-ethnic community because that seemed to be what the political leadership in Zenica wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Zenica being identified as primarily a Muslim-controlled or dominated area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your experience and observation was that by early May of 1993, most of the Croat population was able to move back into the Zenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That was clearly what they were trying to do. I think there was some suggestion that some of the Croats, who had left the Zenica area, moved across to Vitez and who then wanted to return, were being prevented from coming back by the Croats, but I'm not sure exactly why that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 16 and 17, that would be your testimony today, Mr. McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, I think by now, has been touched on, but you affirm that again is a true statement in terms of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we move on, I notice in that paragraph, in inverted commas, the words "by a little bit of extreme violence," I would like to ask the witness this: Are those your words taken out of one of your reports? I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think, sir, that is a comment which I made during one of my previous appearances here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Scott? Is that where that comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It actually came from his testimony in the Blaskic case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 19 would be your testimony today as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've touched on earlier already the three schools of thought that the President asked you about. Did you come to the conclusion, your own conclusion as a result of your work as to which of these schools of thought, based on your investigation, was the most plausible or some that were not plausible?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it's quite clear from what I saw in the conclusion that I reached that it was, if you like, the third school of thought which was that the Croats had initiated a coordinated series of attacks throughout Central Bosnia with a view to changing the ethnic basis of the areas in which they controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see any indication that Serbs had been involved in the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, paragraph 20, other than -- well, first of all, you'd affirm that again this would be your testimony this morning -- this is your testimony this morning?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It's worth pointing out that at this stage, and we debated this at some length last year, the words that "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots" were my summary at the point when I took up writing my note again of what we'd been talking about, as opposed to his words, but that was clearly the impression which I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. My question here is when you went to Vitez in early May and the discussions with Ambassador Thebault and others, you had put together a list of people you hoped or thought you will like to interview; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. Right at the beginning of the trip, I sat down with Jean-Pierre and we worked out who the people were I ought to see to try and get this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Scott, before we go over to that, in paragraph 20, it says in English: "According to the imam of Busovaca," and then there's a quotation, "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots." Apparently, the witness seems to be saying that he's quoting the imam of Busovaca. Is that hearsay? Did he hear directly from the imam? Could we have more details on that sentence? Because in that paragraph, you have one sentence in quotation marks which seems to be a quotation, and it's being attributed to the imam of Busovaca. I would like to know what the link is between the two parts of that paragraph, of that first line of paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I can start with the witness, as the witness just indicated, I think he's trying to be very conscientious about this, the quotation marks around "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots," that is a quotation in the sense that it's being quoted from his own report and from his own notes. I think the witness has indicated, and he can confirm this, the quotation marks are not meant to suggest that those are the exact words of the imam of Busovaca. Before I ask him that, the second part of the statement, the second quote that you reference in paragraph 20, Your Honour, I will just tell you again comes from Mr. McLeod's testimony in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As to the first part, Mr. McLeod, going back to your prior answer, can you clarify that further for Judge Bennouna and for the rest of the Court as to your taking down or referring to that statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly. The writing in inverted commas comes directly out of the report which I wrote. If it will be useful, I can show you my original note that I wrote sitting in the front room of the imam. I actually wrote -- shall we stick it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure. That's fine. For the record and so the Court knows, you're referring to your original handwritten notes from your interviews and from your work?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is the original note written in the notebook as I was writing, taking notes. You can see, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO, Your Honour, but it hasn't been handed out. But I will say that a copy of these notes were provided to the Defence some time ago.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: You can see what I wrote as I was sitting with him "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots." At this stage, six years later, I honestly can't remember whether that was me simply writing down exactly what the imam said or me picking up the flow of the conversation again and just writing for my own reference, summarising what we've just been talking about. On the preceding page, I can show you that the imam had been showing me a pass which he had been issued with, and I'd wrote down the names of the people who had signed the pass, one of them being Mr. Kordic. Having looked at that and written down the names, either he said, "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots," or is it me just summarising, "Kordic seems to be the man calling the shots --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I'm sorry, but on behalf of the reporter, could you please slow down a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You talk quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Keep an eye on the lady in the corner and see if she's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Scott, if I understand correctly, Mr. McLeod, these notes were written down right after the meeting with the imam of Busovaca; is that right? The notes that we are being shown, they were written by you right after the meeting with the imam of Busovaca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wrote these notes during the meeting, so I was sitting with my book on the imam's table, and I was writing as he was speaking. So quite a lot of the notes are exactly what the interpreter was saying as she was translating what he said, and some of the notes are my interjections, as I was just trying to keep track of the conversation as we went. This is written during the conversation rather than after the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna, it might be helpful to you and to the other members of the Court if I could direct your attention to appendix K2, which is the interview statement with the imam, where you can see in appendix K, page 2, and I'm looking to the fifth paragraph on that page, starting with the words, "He has a pass ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You just touched on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I don't have annex K. What page is it exactly? What is the number at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have to say in the version I have, Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's the fifth paragraph from the top starting with the words, "He has a pass ..." which is the next question I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Page 3 in French.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 3 in French, apparently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Second page. In French, it is the last page?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's right before the number 020230.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I heard from the interpreter at one point that it was on page 3 of the French version. The top of the last page of the French version. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you had just mentioned, and I was coming to this in any event, during that interview, did he, the imam, show you a pass that he had been given by certain HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was one of the names on that pass Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back to, in general, paragraph 20, you had indicated a few minutes ago now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said one of the names on the pass was Dario Kordic. In what capacity was it represented there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the reference to Mr. Kordic's position or in what capacity he had signed the pass? For the record, you've put your notes back on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It's page 61, to assist you finding the version you've been given. So you can see I've simply written "He has a pass signed by," and then I've just written down the names, and "Dario Kordic" from the "HDZ." The pass was signed the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You had said a few minutes ago that when you knew you were going to Vitez or perhaps soon after you got there, you prepared some list, either mentally or on paper perhaps, of people who you would want to interview as part of your job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Dario Kordic one of the people on your list?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you think he was one of the people you would want to interview?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was quite clear to the members of ECMM, with whom I was talking, by then he was a key player, a key individual in the events that were taking place around that area. The first occasion where I had come across his name in the context of this report was when I was reading through the ECMM daily reports on events that were taking place while I was sorting out in my own mind, as I had described yesterday, what had happened. There was one event where a UNHCR convoy had been, in my report, I said "highjacked," which is presumably the term which was used in the ECMM report, at Busovaca, and the instruction was given by the Croatian military command to Mr. Kordic to release the convoy. He was the man who had some control over events in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That order was given to Mr. Kordic or Kordic gave the order? If you want to look at your notes, please do.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The order was given to him. Yes. This is my note of the ECMM report as opposed to the original. Presumably someone could get a hold of the original report.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please slow down?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is my note of the ECMM report --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have to object to that, Your Honour, on the grounds of double hearsay. He says that it's a note that he made of an original report that someone else prepared and which he read. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're satisfied this has got the stamp of reliability. This was a note which the witness made in the course of his professional duties of an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at that note then, Mr. McLeod, can you tell us or clarify, perhaps on the ELMO, you can point to which particular entry you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: All right. This is on page R-14, if anybody wants to find it. It's right at the back of the report. So the ECMM report said that the HVO commander in chief, Petkovic, had ordered Mr. Kordic to release the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Petkovic was in the military chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, you didn't wind up talking to Mr. Kordic during that trip, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in conclusion, what happened with your report when it was made? Just in terms of did you report this back to the head of the ECMM, just to finish the story, can you tell the Court what became of your report as you understood it, and was it used as the basis of further actions by the ECMM and the EU?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I got back up to Zagreb on the 12th, 13th of May, finished writing up my report. I started typing up the notes as I was going, but it was finished and published on the 15th, having been proofed and approved by the headquarters of ECMM. Copies were then distributed to each of the delegations who then passed it back to their capitals, I imagine, fairly rapidly. At the same time, Mostar was exploding, I suppose is the neatest way of describing it, and I think there was an EU mission to Mostar. So ECMM was writing a briefing paper for the EU ministers, I think it was the ministers who were going to Mostar, and the basis of my report was used as a key part of that briefing material which was being written by Mr. Andersen, who was the deputy head of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your report, the report which is marked as Exhibit 926, was it accepted by your organisation as a credible and reliable report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I just wanted to follow up on the whole question of the method of preparing your report. You took notes --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- during the meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You returned to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you wrote the report, did you discuss your findings with your superiors?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I did was I wrote a draft of the report. The actual report itself being just the one page at the front, I drafted it and then circulated that draft to Mr. Andersen who was the deputy head of the mission on the political side and the political advisor and I think also to the military -- the chief of staff who had been a Canadian and said, "This is what I think." It was looked at, and in practice, it was turned down slightly because they thought I was being slightly too strong in some of my views. They thought, by the time they had finished with it, that was an acceptable, balanced report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In some cases, changes would have been made to what you originally prepared?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just to the one page at the front. Nobody changed anything that I had written in terms of my write-up of the original notes that I had written during the meetings. I simply sat with my contemporaneous notes and basically copy-typed them so that I would have as close as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In particular, the conclusions that you arrived at, would those have been discussed with your authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Definitely. It was exactly the conclusions which they looked at and they then agreed were acceptable as conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, your objective was to meet with the leading members of the political and military leadership of the three cities or towns that you visited; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was the name of the political leader in Zenica on the Croat side that you met?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't meet a political leader on the Croat side but I met a couple of Catholic priests who were the effective leaders of the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was the name of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, can you remember that this has to be interpreted? Could you take it slowly? Mr. McLeod, also if you would allow a pause before answering and a pause, Mr. Sayers, before the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did not meet any military leaders on the Croat side in Zenica either, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't meet any political leaders in Busovaca, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I had been hoping to meet Mr. Kordic, and I ran out of time, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you didn't meet any political leaders, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you didn't meet any military leaders in Busovaca either, did you? "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let's make sure we get it right. No. They were all policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the three stories or three versions of the Croat story that you've related to Judge May in response to his question, could you just point out to me in exhibit F where they appear during your meeting with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak, because I could not see them in that version of your report, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're referring to the three versions of whether it was a Croatian attack, a Serb attack, or a Serb --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's my summary of the three versions of the story which I was being told by all the various parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: We can, if you like, find the references to either some extremists or a Muslim attack. I think the third version was self-evidently the version being given by various other people. We can go through it line by line if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We will do that, but you would concede, would you not, that in your notes of your interviews with Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak and in your interview with Colonel Blaskic, there isn't any reference to a story about a Serbian agent provacateur, as you put it, is there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we can check, but I'm fairly certain that that was one of the stories which was being put about. I'm quite certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's not the question, sir. Does it appear in your notes? You've read your notes, haven't you, to prepare for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You know that it's not in there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if it's not, I'll take your word for it, sir, but I'm quite sure that that was one of the stories which was being put about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why you would omit something like that from your notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, you were sent down to the Lasva Valley at the age of 30; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your objective was to gather all of the facts in order to come up with a neutral, impartial conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: To gather as many of the facts that I could given the time that was available and the people that were available to see me, but, yes, that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just check off some names of ECMM monitors who were actually present and had been for some time, sir, in the Lasva Valley region. Eric Friis-Pedersen had been stationed there for some months, number of months, had he not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Henk Morsink too?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember him as an individual but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How about Jeremy Fleming?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you meet with him at all during your whirlwind tour through the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Too quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour, to restrain and reign myself in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you keep an eye on the LiveNote reporter to make sure that it's not too quick?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if somebody in the Defence team will undertake to listen to the translation. Keep an eye on how -- or an ear on how the interpreters are doing, and keep control of Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll do my best at self-restraint but I will definitely rely on my colleagues to reign me in if I get out of control, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Jeremy Fleming was the chairman of something called the Busovaca joint coordination commission; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Busovaca joint commission, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Mr. Fleming during your tour through the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I spoke to him while I was there on that occasion, but I certainly did talk to him on a fairly regular basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. Did you talk to him during your tour through the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember whether Jeremy was actually in the theatre at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How about Mr. Torbjorn Junhov? Did you speak to him when you were in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: As an individual, I can't remember whether he was one of the monitors who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dieter Schelschmidt?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, I suspect you're going to run through a list of all the monitors who were there. The two key names that I can remember were Eric Friis-Pedersen, because he was there with me most of the time, and Jean-Pierre Thebault because he was there with me some of the time and he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've testified in Blaskic for a number of days; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in the Aleksovski case; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've got the experience of a prosecutor court martial yourself, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're familiar with the process of questions and answers in cross-examination; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you travelled to the area on May the 3rd?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You spent May the 7th through the 11th interviewing people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then headed back to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You wrote your one-page report on May the 15th?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was probably written on the 14th and discussed but published on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You'd spent the Christmas of 1992 at the headquarters of General Morillon in Kiseljak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You spent about a month in Kiseljak, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Drove occasionally up the road through Busovaca to Zenica from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once rather than occasionally, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You passed through the Muslim checkpoint at Kacuni and Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware that I was stopped at any point. I might have to check a map to find out exactly where the places are that you're referring to, but if there were checkpoints there, yes, I would have driven through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Kordic during that one-month sojourn?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Maric, Zoran Maric, from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Ivica Rajic from Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, do you know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you -- forgive me. The Croatian Community, could you give me that in terms of HDZ? Is that what you're referring to or just more broadly the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll be very simple: No, because I'm not quite sure what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the HDZ is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the HDZ, my understanding is that it's the political party which represented the majority of Croats in that area. So I would call it HDZ rather than the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the HVO is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll slow down. The HVO is or was the Croatian military formation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of the HVO was at the time that you were travelling through the Lasva Valley during mid May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'd just like to show the witness an extract from the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which I've shared with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D20/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question about this document. This is a copy of a decree published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in March of 1993. The decree is actually dated the 26th of February, 1993, and I'd just like you to turn to the third page. Do you recognise the name Jadranko Prlic as the president of the HVO HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're hearing that name for the first time today, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I honestly can't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never met Dr. Jadranko Prlic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've never asked for permission to meet him from anyone who has the power to arrange such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let us turn a little bit to your report, sir. As I understand it, the first thing that you did was to assemble all of the papers that you would need to basically provide yourself with a background of the task before you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The first thing that you did was to acquire copies of the European Community Monitoring Mission reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They're in a daily report format, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They don't look like exhibit R to your report, do they, at all?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: The reports were based -- they were typed on -- we had a system called capsat. It's a computer which would fire off reports using satellites. So they came in a number of various different forms, but I'm sure you have one there for us to look at anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree with me that the summary of reports that you put in as exhibit R, those are just snippets, little extracts, from much more lengthy reports that the ECMM prepared every day; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. I was attempting just to summarise the key events and locations rather than actually copying complete reports which contained all sorts of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So rather than attaching those reports to your -- or the ECMM daily reports to your report, what you did was you went through and took out little snippets of reports from various dates yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to point out that we've actually made a request to the Prosecution for full copies of those reports and that request has been declined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The second source of documents that you looked at, sir, I believe, was UNPROFOR reports. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those are kept in what kind of a format?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again, those were -- the copies that I had were paper reports produced in a standard military situation report format, and I was going through those, attempting to find the relevant and key information and just identifying what had happened and where it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you were provided with a series of situation reports, daily sit-reps, from the military authorities in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Those are shared with ECMM, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who gave you those?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: From memory, I think that I was using both those which ECMM had and possibly some that were provided by BritBat, but I can't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the British regiment that was present in Vitez was the 1st Cheshire regiment, I believe?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a document called a military information summary or a milinfosum, for short?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: I should think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you ever given any milinfosums by the 1st Cheshire Regiment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I can't remember whether they were milinfosums or just the sit-reps, but I was given their summary of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it that in compiling exhibit R or appendix R to your report, you've deployed the same technique of taking snippets out of the sit-reps and the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You didn't put the full reports in here?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
